Alton Augustus Adams

Biography

Alton Augustus Adams, Sr.

Bandmaster, Composer, and Trailblazer — The Sound of the Virgin Islands

A World Being Born

When Alton Augustus Adams came into the world on November 4, 1889, in Charlotte Amalie, the capital of the island of St. Thomas, the territory known as the Danish West Indies was still a colonial possession of the Kingdom of Denmark. The Caribbean at the close of the 19th century was a patchwork of European empires: British, French, Dutch, Danish, and Spanish flags flew over islands whose populations — the overwhelming majority of them descended from enslaved Africans — were navigating the treacherous terrain between legal emancipation and true social equality.

St. Thomas, even under Danish rule, was a cosmopolitan place. Its magnificent natural harbor had made Charlotte Amalie a vital entrepôt for Caribbean trade, and the island's population was a cultural mosaic of African-descended islanders, Danish officials, merchants of multiple nationalities, and immigrants from across the region. It was in this layered, vibrant, music-saturated world that Adams grew up — absorbing not only the sounds of European brass-band tradition but also the rhythms of the Caribbean: the bamboula, the quadrille, the calypso, and the hymns that rang from the island's many churches.

Early Life: The Self-Made Musician

Adams's parents were artisans — working people who shaped material into something useful with their hands — and they passed that ethic of craft and self-reliance on to their son. As a young man, Adams apprenticed as both a carpenter and a shoemaker, learning trades that would provide economic security. But music was pulling at him irresistibly.

His musical education was largely self-directed, a testament to extraordinary determination in an era when formal music instruction was not readily available to Black Caribbean youth. He taught himself to play multiple instruments — the piccolo, flute, clarinet, cornet, and trombone — working through the mechanics of each with the same systematic patience he might have brought to carpentry. He supplemented this autodidactic practice with rigorous study of music theory, ultimately enrolling in a correspondence course with Dr. Hugh A. Clarke at the University of Pennsylvania — a remarkable arrangement that allowed him to receive instruction from a leading American music theorist without ever leaving his Caribbean island.

His appetite for learning extended beyond music. Adams became a prolific writer and journalist, contributing articles to publications including Jacobs' Band Monthly and The Dominant, and later editing The Herald in St. Croix. He understood instinctively that music needed advocates — people who could explain its value, interpret its history, and make the case for its place in the life of a community.

The St. Thomas Municipal Band and the Adams Juvenile Band

In 1906, Adams joined the St. Thomas Municipal Band, the leading musical institution on the island. Here he received his first formal experience of ensemble playing and musical leadership, absorbing the brass-band tradition that would define his life's work.

By 1910, Adams had struck out on his own. He founded the Adams Juvenile Band — an ensemble composed of young people between the ages of 8 and 18 drawn from Charlotte Amalie and its surroundings. The decision to work with youth was not merely practical; it was philosophical. Adams believed that musical training was inseparable from character formation, discipline, and community pride. The Juvenile Band performed regularly at civic events throughout Charlotte Amalie, giving free concerts at Emancipation Garden — the square named for the 1848 emancipation of enslaved people on the Danish West Indies, a space charged with the memory of freedom.

Within a few years, the Adams Juvenile Band had become one of the most celebrated musical ensembles in the region, admired not only for technical proficiency but for the social statement it represented: Black youth from a Caribbean island, competing on equal or superior terms with any band in the Western Hemisphere.

Transfer Day and the Leap into the U.S. Navy

The world that made Alton Adams changed forever in 1917, when the United States purchased the Danish West Indies for $25 million in gold — transforming the islands overnight from a Danish colony into American territory. For the residents of St. Thomas, St. Croix, and St. John, the transfer was disorienting: new laws, new currency, new administrators, new expectations. The U.S. Navy assumed governance of the territory, and Black islanders — many of whom had hoped American rule might bring greater civil rights — soon found themselves navigating a segregated military bureaucracy.

In this context, Adams's band became something far more than a musical ensemble. On June 2, 1917, Alton Augustus Adams and his entire Adams Juvenile Band were formally enlisted into the United States Navy. Adams was appointed to the rank of Chief Petty Officer, making him simultaneously the first Black bandmaster in the United States Navy and one of the first African Americans to hold that rating in the modern U.S. naval establishment.

The significance of this moment extended far beyond military paperwork. The U.S. Navy of 1917 was a deeply segregated institution. African Americans served in limited roles, often as mess attendants. Adams's appointment as a Chief Petty Officer in charge of an official Navy band was, by any measure, an extraordinary exception — one made possible partly because the geographic and demographic reality of St. Thomas made it impossible to staff a naval band any other way, but made meaningful by Adams's undeniable excellence.

"He was not just making music. He was making history every time he raised his baton." — Naval History and Heritage Command

Wartime Service, Concert Tours, and Cultural Diplomacy

Adams served the U.S. Navy through both World War I and World War II — a span of service that speaks to both his indispensability and his extraordinary longevity as a bandmaster. During these decades, his band did far more than provide ceremonial music. The ensemble functioned as what historians have called a "cultural bridge" between the white naval administration and the predominantly Black population of the Virgin Islands — a human connection point at a time when racial tensions in the new American territory ran high.

Beyond the Caribbean, Adams took his band on the road. In 1924, the band undertook a landmark concert tour of the U.S. eastern seaboard, performing in Washington, D.C., Philadelphia, New York, and Boston to widespread acclaim. These performances placed Caribbean Black musicians before American audiences in a context of dignity and excellence — a quiet but powerful refutation of prevailing racial stereotypes. The band also performed at the White House, a summit of ceremonial honor that few American musicians of any race achieved.

Adams's compositions were performed by some of the leading ensembles of the era, including the celebrated Goldman Band in New York — the premier outdoor concert band in America. John Philip Sousa himself, the reigning king of American band music, was familiar with Adams's work. Adams contributed articles on band music to national publications, argued for the artistic seriousness of the band medium, and was recognized by peers across the country as a master of his craft.

The Virgin Islands March: A Nation's Anthem

Of all Adams's compositions — and he produced many, including marches, waltzes, bamboulas, and solo pieces — none achieved greater cultural permanence than the "Virgin Islands March," composed in 1919. Written in the sweeping, confident style of Sousa, the march captured both the martial pride of the islands' new American identity and something distinctly Caribbean in its rhythmic vitality.

The march was quickly adopted as an unofficial anthem among islanders. Decades later, in 1963, it was formally designated the official territorial anthem of the U.S. Virgin Islands — a status it holds to this day, played at government ceremonies, sporting events, and public gatherings across St. Thomas, St. Croix, and St. John.

Other notable compositions included "The Governor's Own," "Warbling in the Moonlight," and "Spirit of the U.S.N." — works that showcased Adams's fluency across different registers of American band music, from patriotic grandeur to lyrical elegance.

Legacy: Educator, Civic Builder, and Cultural Pioneer

Adams retired from the U.S. Navy in 1947 after three decades of service. But retirement from the military meant no retreat from public life. Adams turned his energies to the broader project of building the Virgin Islands as a community.

He was instrumental in developing public-school music education programs in the territory — working to ensure that the next generation of Virgin Islanders would have access to the formal musical training he himself had pursued through sheer determination. He became a charter member and longtime president of the Virgin Islands Hotel Association, serving in that role for 19 years and helping to shape the territory's emerging tourism economy. He was also a founder of the Caribbean Travel Association, an organization that helped promote the region as a destination at a time when Caribbean tourism was in its infancy.

In 1978, Fisk University — the historic HBCU in Nashville, Tennessee — awarded Adams an Honorary Doctor of Humane Letters, recognizing his lifetime of contributions to music as composer, conductor, and educator.

Adams had been nominated for membership in the American Bandmasters Association as early as 1936 — a nomination that, in a reflection of the racial climate of the era, was initially rejected. Posthumously, the Association honored him with its "Alton Adams Legacy Recognition," acknowledging the debt American band music owed to the man who had been excluded from its ranks by prejudice.

Perhaps most movingly, in 2016 — nearly three decades after his death — the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture (NMAAHC) inducted artifacts from Adams's career into its permanent "Musical Crossroads" exhibit. Among the items: his flute and piccolo, the very instruments he had played at the formal ceremonial transfer of the Virgin Islands from Denmark to the United States in 1917. Alongside them: his Virgin Islands Medal of Honor and the ceremonial cape from his honorary doctorate ceremony. These objects now rest among the most treasured artifacts of African American cultural history — fitting homes for instruments that once helped a man and his community find their voice.

Alton Augustus Adams, Sr. died on November 23, 1987, at the age of 98 — having lived long enough to see his "Virgin Islands March" become an official anthem, his band's induction into military history acknowledged, and his community's pride in him openly celebrated. He was a carpenter's son who built something far more enduring than wood: a legacy of music, dignity, and possibility for the people of the U.S. Virgin Islands and for Black Americans throughout the military and beyond.

"His was a life lived in full — as a musician, a teacher, a civic leader, and an American who refused to let the limits others imposed on him define what he could achieve." — U.S. Navy Memorial Foundation

Major Contributions

  • Alton Augustus Adams made landmark contributions across music, military history, education, and civic life in the U.
  • S.
  • Virgin Islands and the United States at large.
  • As the **first Black bandmaster in the United States Navy**, appointed in 1917 when he and his Adams Juvenile Band were enlisted following the American purchase of the Danish West Indies, Adams broke a racial barrier in the U.
  • S.
  • military decades before formal desegregation.
  • His appointment as Chief Petty Officer made him one of the first African Americans to hold that rating.
  • During his 30-year naval career spanning both World Wars, Adams served not only as a musical director but as a cultural diplomat — his band bridging racial and institutional divides between white naval administrators and the predominantly Black Virgin Islands population.
  • As a composer, Adams's most enduring achievement is the **"Virgin Islands March"** (1919), formally adopted as the official territorial anthem of the U.
  • S.
  • Virgin Islands in 1963 — a piece played at government ceremonies and public occasions to this day.
  • His works were performed by premier American ensembles including the Goldman Band of New York.
  • Beyond performance and composition, Adams devoted himself to building institutions: he helped establish music education in Virgin Islands public schools, co-founded the Caribbean Travel Association, and served for 19 years as president of the Virgin Islands Hotel Association, helping shape the territory's modern tourism economy.
  • In 2016, the Smithsonian's NMAAHC enshrined his instruments and medals in its permanent collection, cementing his place in the national African American cultural heritage.
